_comment: Essential commands for each topic that are not (yet) taught in a lesson. Merged into the Commands reference page by CommandController, and shown with an 'Extra' badge. Keyed by topic slug.

network-devices.example:
R1# show cdp neighbors
Device ID  Local Intrfce  Holdtme  Capability  Platform  Port ID
SW1        Gig 0/0        143      S I         WS-C3560  Gig 0/1
network-devices.description: Lists directly connected Cisco devices discovered by CDP, showing the local and remote interface, the device type and the platform.
network-devices.note: CDP is Cisco proprietary and enabled by default. It is the fastest way to map an unfamiliar network.

network-devices.description: Adds the neighbour's IP address and full IOS version to the summary output — useful when you need to Telnet or SSH onward to a device you have not documented.
network-devices.note: show cdp entry <device-id> shows the detail for one specific neighbour.

network-devices.description: Disables CDP globally on the device. Because CDP advertises platform and version information, it is normally disabled on interfaces facing untrusted networks.
network-devices.note: no cdp enable in interface config mode disables CDP on one interface only.

network-devices.description: Enables LLDP, the vendor-neutral (IEEE 802.1AB) equivalent of CDP. Unlike CDP it is disabled by default on Cisco devices.
network-devices.note: Use LLDP in multi-vendor networks where CDP will not see non-Cisco devices.
lldp transmit and lldp receive control LLDP per interface and can be set independently.

interfaces-and-cables.description: Shows the IOS version, uptime, hardware model, installed interfaces, amount of memory and the configuration register.
interfaces-and-cables.note: The first command to run on an unfamiliar device.

interfaces-and-cables.description: Lists what an interface physically supports — the speeds, duplex settings and media types available on that port.
interfaces-and-cables.note: Useful for confirming whether a port can actually run at the speed you are trying to configure.

interfaces-and-cables.description: Lists only the ports currently in the err-disabled state, together with the reason each one was disabled.
Enables automatic MDI/MDIX crossover detection, so the port works with either a straight-through or a crossover cable.
interfaces-and-cables.note: Enabled by default on modern switches, which is why cable type rarely matters any more.

tcp-ip-model.description: Lists the device's active TCP connections with local and remote socket addresses and connection state.
tcp-ip-model.note: Shows the transport layer in action — each entry is an IP address and port pair.

tcp-ip-model.description: Lists a host's open TCP and UDP sockets with their local and foreign addresses and states — the host-side view of the transport layer.
tcp-ip-model.note: A host OS command, not Cisco IOS.

tcp-ip-model.description: Queries DNS to resolve a hostname to an IP address, demonstrating the application layer service that almost all traffic depends on.
Tells the Cisco device which DNS server to use when resolving names typed at the CLI.
tcp-ip-model.note: Pair with ip domain-lookup. Many engineers instead run no ip domain-lookup to stop the router trying to resolve mistyped commands.

ios-cli.example:
R1(config)# line console 0
R1(config-line)# password cisco
R1(config-line)# login
ios-cli.description: Enters line configuration mode for the console port, where the console password is set. login tells the device to actually prompt for it.
ios-cli.note: Without the login command the password is configured but never requested.

ios-cli.example:
R1(config)# line vty 0 4
R1(config-line)# login local
R1(config-line)# transport input ssh
ios-cli.description: Configures the virtual terminal lines used for Telnet and SSH sessions. The numbers are how many simultaneous remote sessions are allowed.
ios-cli.note: transport input ssh restricts the lines to SSH, blocking plain-text Telnet.

ios-cli.description: Creates a local user account with a hashed password, for use with login local on the vty or console lines.
ios-cli.note: username ... password stores the password in plain text — prefer secret.

ios-cli.example:
R1(config)# ip domain-name example.com
R1(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
ios-cli.description: Generates the RSA key pair that SSH requires. A hostname and a domain name must be configured first, because they form the key's name.
ios-cli.note: A modulus of at least 768 bits is required for SSH version 2; 2048 is the sensible modern choice.

ios-cli.description: Forces the device to accept only SSH version 2, which is the secure version.
Stops the device treating a mistyped command as a hostname and trying to resolve it via DNS — which otherwise hangs the CLI for a minute.
ios-cli.note: One of the first commands most engineers type in a lab.

ios-cli.description: Stops console log messages from interrupting what you are typing — the command line is reprinted after any message appears.
Sets how long a session can be idle before it is logged out automatically. 0 0 disables the timeout entirely.
ios-cli.note: Disabling the timeout is convenient in a lab but a security risk in production.

ios-cli.description: Sets the message-of-the-day banner shown before login. Legally important: it is how unauthorised access is warned against.
ios-cli.note: The delimiter can be any character not used in the message itself.

ios-cli.description: Removes the --More-- pagination so long output scrolls out in one go — ideal when capturing a full configuration.
ios-cli.note: Applies to the current session only.

ios-cli.description: Lists the contents of flash memory, including the IOS image files and their sizes.
Deletes the saved configuration from NVRAM. Followed by a reload, this returns the device to factory defaults.
ios-cli.note: On a switch also delete vlan.dat, or the VLAN database will survive the reset.

ios-cli.description: Restarts the device. reload in 5 schedules a restart in five minutes — a safety net when making a risky remote change, as the device will reboot to the saved config if you lock yourself out.
ios-cli.note: reload cancel aborts a scheduled reload once you have confirmed the change worked.

ios-cli.description: Lists the recently entered commands for the current session.
ios-cli.note: The up and down arrow keys, or Ctrl+P and Ctrl+N, recall them one at a time.

ethernet-lan-switching.example: SW1(config)# mac address-table static aaaa.aa00.0001 vlan 10 interface g0/1
ethernet-lan-switching.description: Manually pins a MAC address to a port and VLAN. The entry never ages out and is not affected by clear mac address-table dynamic.
Sets how long an unused dynamic MAC entry is kept before being removed. The default is 300 seconds.
Shows how many dynamic, static and total MAC addresses are in the table, and how much table space remains.
ethernet-lan-switching.note: A sudden spike in dynamic entries can indicate a MAC flooding attack.

ethernet-lan-switching.description: Per-interface totals of frames in and out; the errors form shows CRC errors, runts, giants and collisions.
ethernet-lan-switching.note: Rising CRC errors usually mean a cabling or duplex problem. Collisions on a full-duplex link indicate a duplex mismatch.

ethernet-lan-switching.description: Resets interface statistics to zero so you can see whether errors are still increasing right now, rather than having accumulated over months of uptime.

ip-addressing.description: Makes the interface obtain its IPv4 address from a DHCP server instead of using a static address.
ip-addressing.note: Common on the outside interface of a small-office router.

ip-addressing.description: Adds an additional IP address to an interface so it can serve two subnets on the same physical network.

ip-addressing.syntax:
interface vlan <vlan-id>
 ip address <address> <mask>
 no shutdown
ip-addressing.example:
SW1(config)# interface vlan 1
SW1(config-if)# ip address 192.168.1.10 255.255.255.0
SW1(config-if)# no shutdown
ip-addressing.description: Gives a Layer 2 switch a management IP address, so it can be reached by SSH, Telnet or SNMP. The switch still does not route.
ip-addressing.note: A Layer 2 switch has exactly one active management SVI.

ip-addressing.description: Tells a Layer 2 switch where to send management traffic destined off its own subnet.
ip-addressing.note: Only used when ip routing is disabled. A Layer 3 switch uses a default route instead.

ip-addressing.description: Detailed Layer 3 information for an interface: address, broadcast address, MTU, and which features such as access lists or proxy ARP are active.
ip-addressing.note: Different from show ip interface brief, which is only a one-line summary.

ip-addressing.description: Shows each router hop along the path to a destination, which is how you find where connectivity actually breaks.
ip-addressing.note: On Windows the command is tracert.

switch-interfaces.example:
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport port-security
switch-interfaces.description: Enables port security, restricting which and how many MAC addresses may send frames into the port.
switch-interfaces.note: The port must be a static access or trunk port first — port security cannot be enabled on a dynamic (DTP) port.

switch-interfaces.description: Sets how many MAC addresses the port may learn. The default is 1.
switch-interfaces.note: Allow 2 where an IP phone and a PC share a port.

switch-interfaces.description: Learns the connected device's MAC address dynamically and writes it into the running configuration, so it persists if saved.
switch-interfaces.note: Remember to save, or sticky addresses are lost on reload.

switch-interfaces.description: Chooses what happens on a violation: shutdown err-disables the port (the default), restrict drops the traffic and logs it, protect drops it silently.
switch-interfaces.note: Exam point: only shutdown and restrict generate a log message and increment the violation counter.

switch-interfaces.description: Shows the port security configuration and status: violation mode, maximum and current MAC count, and the violation counter.

switch-interfaces.syntax:
interface range <range>
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan <unused-vlan>
 shutdown
switch-interfaces.example:
SW1(config)# interface range f0/13-24
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 999
SW1(config-if-range)# shutdown
switch-interfaces.description: The standard hardening recipe for unused switch ports: force them to access mode, park them in an unused black-hole VLAN, and shut them down.

ipv4-header.description: Sends a ping with the Don't Fragment flag set. If the packet is too large for a link along the path it is dropped rather than fragmented, which is how you discover the real path MTU.
ipv4-header.note: Directly exercises the DF bit in the IPv4 header's Flags field.

ipv4-header.description: Sends a specific number of echo requests instead of the default five — useful for spotting intermittent loss.
Sets the largest packet the interface will send. mtu applies to the whole frame; ip mtu applies to IPv4 packets only.
ipv4-header.note: Lowering the IP MTU is a common fix for tunnels, where extra headers push packets over the physical limit.

ipv4-header.example:
R1# debug ip packet detail
R1# undebug all
ipv4-header.description: Prints per-packet information as the router processes it, including source, destination and protocol from the IPv4 header.
ipv4-header.note: Use with great care on a live device — it is CPU intensive and can overwhelm a busy router. Always follow with undebug all.

ipv4-header.description: Summarises IP statistics, including counts of fragmented packets, bad checksums and TTL-expired packets.

routing.example:
R1# show ip route 192.168.4.10
Routing entry for 192.168.4.0/24
routing.description: Shows exactly which routing table entry would be used for one specific destination — the quickest way to confirm longest-prefix matching.
routing.note: Far more reliable than reading the whole table and guessing which route wins.

routing.description: Lists every route that falls inside the given range — useful for checking summarisation.
Summarises every dynamic routing protocol running on the device: which networks it advertises, its neighbours, and its administrative distance.
Flushes the routing table and forces it to be rebuilt.
routing.note: Disruptive on a production router — routes are relearned, which briefly interrupts forwarding.

routing.description: Adds a backup static route with a worse administrative distance. It stays out of the routing table until the preferred route disappears — a floating static route.
routing.note: Default administrative distances: connected 0, static 1, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, RIP 120.

routing.description: Enables IPv6 routing. A router forwards IPv4 by default but will not forward IPv6 until this is configured.
routing.note: The IPv6 counterpart of the ip routing requirement on a Layer 3 switch.

routing.description: Creates an IPv6 static route. The structure mirrors ip route, except the prefix length is written in slash notation.
routing.note: The IPv6 default route is ::/0, the equivalent of 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0.

life-of-a-packet.description: Reveals every Layer 3 hop a packet passes through, which is the life of a packet made visible.
life-of-a-packet.note: It works by sending packets with increasing TTL values and collecting the ICMP Time Exceeded replies.

life-of-a-packet.description: Shows the IP-to-MAC mappings the router knows. Every hop must resolve the next hop's MAC address before it can build the frame.
life-of-a-packet.note: clear arp-cache empties the table and forces fresh ARP requests.

life-of-a-packet.description: Shows the Cisco Express Forwarding table — the optimised structure the router actually consults when forwarding, derived from the routing and ARP tables.

subnetting.group: Checking your maths on a device
subnetting.description: Lists the addresses actually configured, so you can confirm your subnet plan matches the deployment.

subnetting.group: Checking your maths on a device
subnetting.description: A summary (aggregate) route covers several contiguous subnets with one entry — the practical payoff of understanding VLSM and CIDR.
subnetting.note: The summary mask must be short enough to cover every subnet but no shorter, or you will attract traffic for addresses you do not own.

subnetting.group: Checking your maths on a device
subnetting.description: Shows a host's address, subnet mask and default gateway — the three values your subnet plan has to get right.
subnetting.note: A wrong mask is a classic cause of a host that can reach some destinations but not others.

vlans.description: Shows the detail for one VLAN only, including every port assigned to it.
The definitive per-port Layer 2 view: administrative and operational mode, access VLAN, native VLAN and the allowed VLAN list.
vlans.note: Use this when a port is not behaving as the configuration suggests it should.

vlans.example:
SW1(config-if)# switchport mode access
SW1(config-if)# switchport access vlan 10
SW1(config-if)# switchport voice vlan 20
vlans.description: Lets one access port carry both an untagged data VLAN for the PC and a tagged voice VLAN for an IP phone daisy-chained in front of it.
vlans.note: A common exam scenario: the port is an access port, yet it carries two VLANs.

vlans.description: Forces even native VLAN frames to be tagged on trunks, which defeats VLAN hopping by double tagging.
vlans.note: The usual alternative is to set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN that carries no hosts.

vlans.description: Administratively disables a whole VLAN. All traffic in it stops and any SVI for it goes down.
vlans.note: One of the four conditions an SVI needs to reach up/up is that its VLAN is not shut down.

dtp-and-vtp.description: Shows the DTP state of a port, including the negotiation timers and how many DTP frames have been exchanged.
Stops broadcast and unknown-unicast flooding for a VLAN being sent down trunks toward switches that have no ports in that VLAN, saving bandwidth.
dtp-and-vtp.note: Configured on a VTP server and propagated to the whole domain.

dtp-and-vtp.description: Displays the configured VTP domain password.
dtp-and-vtp.note: A mismatched password is a frequent reason a switch silently fails to join the domain.

dtp-and-vtp.syntax:
vtp mode transparent
vtp mode server
dtp-and-vtp.example:
SW1(config)# vtp mode transparent
SW1(config)# vtp mode server
dtp-and-vtp.description: Switching to transparent mode and back resets the configuration revision number to zero.
dtp-and-vtp.note: Always do this before connecting a used switch to a live network — otherwise a high revision number can overwrite the entire domain's VLAN database.

spanning-tree.description: One-screen overview: the STP mode in use, which optional features are enabled by default, and how many ports are blocking, listening, learning and forwarding per VLAN.
Lists, for every VLAN, the root bridge ID, the root path cost, the root port and the current timer values.
spanning-tree.note: The fastest way to confirm the root bridge is where you intended it to be.

spanning-tree.description: Lists only the ports STP is currently blocking — the places where your redundant links are being held in reserve.
Sets how often BPDUs are sent. The default is 2 seconds.
spanning-tree.note: Timers are dictated by the root bridge, so configure them there.

spanning-tree.description: Sets how long a port spends in each of the listening and learning states. The default is 15 seconds each.
spanning-tree.note: Max age 20 + listening 15 + learning 15 = the well-known 50 second convergence time.

spanning-tree.description: Sets how long a switch keeps a BPDU before deciding the neighbour is gone. The default is 20 seconds.
Tells Rapid PVST+ the link is point-to-point so it can use the fast proposal/agreement handshake instead of waiting out the timers.
spanning-tree.note: Inferred from duplex: full duplex is treated as point-to-point, half duplex as shared.

spanning-tree.description: Forces a port that fell back to legacy 802.1D to retry Rapid PVST+, after the old switch that caused the fallback has been removed.

stp-toolkit.description: Lists every port currently blocked by Root Guard, Loop Guard or a native VLAN mismatch, with the inconsistency type for each.
stp-toolkit.note: The single best command for auditing the STP toolkit across a switch.

stp-toolkit.description: Lists every condition the switch will err-disable a port for, and whether detection is enabled for each.
stp-toolkit.note: Pairs with show errdisable recovery, which shows whether automatic recovery is enabled.

stp-toolkit.description: Enables automatic recovery for every err-disable cause at once, rather than naming them one by one.
stp-toolkit.note: Convenient, but it can mask a genuine fault that keeps re-triggering. Prefer enabling specific causes.

stp-toolkit.description: Err-disables ports when it detects an EtherChannel that has been misconfigured on one side only — a common cause of Layer 2 loops.
stp-toolkit.note: Enabled by default on most switches.

stp-toolkit.description: UDLD detects unidirectional links by exchanging keepalives and can disable the port. It solves the same problem as Loop Guard, but by detecting the fault directly rather than reacting to missing BPDUs.
stp-toolkit.note: UDLD and Loop Guard are complementary and are often deployed together on fibre links.
